q: Which new tablet caused his cough?
s: Mr. Adel, 54, started tablets for high blood pressure and a weak heart two months ago. Since then he has a dry, tickly cough that keeps him awake at night. He has no fever and no phlegm, and his chest X-ray is clear. He doesn't smoke. His sugar is controlled on the same metformin he has taken for years. At the same visit his doctor also added a water tablet and a low-dose aspirin.
c: A dry cough that began with the new heart tablets, with a clear chest and no sign of infection.

a.w: ACE inhibitors stop the breakdown of bradykinin, which builds up in the airway and causes a dry cough in about 1 in 10 people.
He has taken it for years without a cough, and its side effects are in the gut.
A water tablet causes low potassium and frequent urination, not a cough.
Aspirin can trigger wheeze in some people with asthma, but not a dry cough with a clear chest.

lq: Which blood pressure drug group commonly causes a dry cough?

q: What cleared her skin?
s: Nour, 19, had deep, painful lumps and cysts on her face and back that left scars. Two courses of antibiotic tablets and several creams did not help. Her doctor asked for two pregnancy tests first, and blood tests for her liver and fats before each monthly refill. After five months her skin was clear, though her lips were dry and cracked the whole time.
c: Scarring acne after failed antibiotics, monthly pregnancy and liver tests, and cracked lips.

a.w: A vitamin A tablet for severe acne. It dries the skin and lips, can harm an unborn baby, and can raise liver enzymes and fats, hence the tests.
She already failed antibiotic tablets, and it doesn't need monthly pregnancy and liver tests.
A cream for mild acne. It wouldn't clear deep cysts or need blood tests.
It can help hormonal acne, but it doesn't crack the lips or need liver and fat tests.

lq: Which acne tablet needs pregnancy tests and causes cracked lips?

q: What was done in the operation?
s: Yusuf, 4, had poor hearing and slow speech for most of a year, with dull, fluid-filled eardrums on both sides. His nursery said he ignored the teacher. He had a short operation under general anesthesia and went home the same day. His hearing got better that same week. Nine months later his mother found a tiny plastic tube on his pillow.
c: Long-lasting fluid behind both eardrums, a day-case operation, and a tiny tube that fell out months later.

a.w: Small tubes in the eardrum let air in and fluid out, so hearing returns. They fall out by themselves after 6 to 12 months.
Taking out the tonsils doesn't drain the middle ear and leaves no tube.
It is for deep nerve deafness, not fluid, and it sits under the skin and never falls out.
Removing the adenoids can help glue ear, but it leaves no tube to fall out.

lq: What operation treats long-lasting glue ear in children?

q: What is in the drip?
s: Hala, 17, was brought in by her sister six hours after swallowing a whole box of painkillers after a fight at home. She feels a little sick but otherwise looks well. Her blood level of the drug sits above the treatment line on the chart. Her liver tests are still normal. The doctor starts a drip that runs for about 21 hours.
c: A big overdose that looks harmless at first, a drug level read against the hours since, and a drip over about 21 hours.

a.w: The antidote for paracetamol overdose. It refills glutathione so the liver can clear the toxic product. The usual course is about 21 hours.
It reverses opioids. She isn't drowsy and her breathing is fine.
It reverses benzodiazepines and is rarely used, because it can cause fits.
It only helps within about an hour of the overdose, and it is drunk, not a drip.

lq: What is the antidote for paracetamol overdose?

q: What had she been taking?
s: Mrs. Salwa, 58, comes to the ER weak, dizzy and vomiting. Her pressure is 78/40 and her sodium is low. Her husband says she has "a lung disease" and took a tablet every morning for months. Last week she felt better, ran out, and didn't refill it. Her blood sugar is normal, her ECG is fine, and she has no fever.
c: A daily tablet for months for a lung disease, stopped a week ago, then low pressure and low sodium.

a.w: Long-term steroids switch off her own adrenal glands. Stopping them suddenly leaves her with no cortisol: an adrenal crisis.
Stopping it raises the sugar, and hers is normal.
Stopping it causes a fast heart and high pressure, not low.
It is an inhaler, not a tablet, and stopping it doesn't drop the pressure.

lq: What happens when long-term steroids are stopped suddenly?

q: What was done through the camera?
s: Mr. Samir, 61, has cirrhosis from hepatitis C. He came in vomiting fresh blood with a pressure of 90/55. He was given blood, a terlipressin drip and antibiotics. That night a camera was passed down his food pipe and the bleeding stopped. Two weeks later swallowing hurt a little, and a second camera showed small healing ulcers where the work had been done.
c: Cirrhosis, fresh blood vomited, a camera down the food pipe, then small ulcers at the treated spots.

a.w: Rubber bands tie off the swollen veins in the food pipe. The banded spots fall off and leave small ulcers that heal.
A tube inside the liver, placed through a neck vein, not a camera. It leaves no ulcers in the food pipe.
A balloon that presses on the veins as a short bridge. It isn't done through the camera.
An open operation that isn't used for bleeding food pipe veins.

lq: What is the first camera treatment for bleeding food pipe varices?

q: What kept Omar well?
s: Baby Omar's heel-prick test on day 5 showed a high level of one building block of protein. His parents were told to start a special formula straight away and, later, a strict low-protein diet with a medical drink. He is now 6, at a normal school and doing well. His older cousin, born abroad without the test, has learning problems and a musty smell.
c: A high protein building block on the newborn heel test, a strict low-protein diet, and a cousin harmed without it.

a.w: In phenylketonuria the body can't break down phenylalanine. Cutting it from birth prevents brain damage.
It is for celiac disease, which the heel test doesn't find and which doesn't harm the brain this way.
They treat an underactive thyroid from birth, also found on the heel test, but that is a hormone, not a diet.
They are used for storage diseases such as Gaucher, not for this.

lq: What is the treatment for phenylketonuria?

q: Which blood thinner did the antibiotic make too strong?
s: Mrs. Amal, 72, has an irregular heartbeat and has taken the same dose of a blood thinner for years with steady results. Last week her doctor gave her an antibiotic for a chest infection. Today she has big bruises on her arms and her gums bleed when she brushes. Her INR, normally 2.5, is now 7.8. She hasn't changed her diet.
c: A blood thinner checked by INR, and an INR that jumped after an antibiotic.

a.w: Antibiotics such as clarithromycin slow how the liver clears warfarin, so the INR rises and she bleeds.
It isn't checked by INR, and a raised INR points to warfarin.
It stops platelets but doesn't raise the INR.
Also a platelet drug, and the INR stays normal.

lq: Which blood thinner is checked by INR and pushed up by many antibiotics?

q: Which antibiotic did they give?
s: Karim, 18, has a sore throat, a fever and big, tender neck glands. His tonsils are covered in white patches and he feels very tired. The clinic gave him an antibiotic. Two days later he has an itchy red rash all over his body. A blood test later shows glandular fever. He has never had a rash from any medicine before.
c: Glandular fever and a rash all over the body two days after an antibiotic.

a.w: In glandular fever, amoxicillin causes a widespread rash in most patients. It isn't a true allergy.
It doesn't cause this typical rash in glandular fever.
Its well-known problem is diarrhea from C. difficile, not a rash.
It isn't used for a sore throat, and its known problems are tendons and heart rhythm.

lq: Which antibiotic gives a rash in glandular fever?

q: What should be given first?
s: Mr. Hamdy, 58, has dialysis three times a week but missed two sessions because of a family funeral. He feels weak and his heartbeat feels slow. His potassium is 7.4, and his ECG shows tall, peaked T waves and wide QRS complexes. A drip line is in. Dialysis can start in about two hours.
c: Very high potassium with ECG changes: the heart needs protecting before anything else.

a.w: It steadies the heart muscle within minutes. It doesn't lower potassium, so insulin with glucose and dialysis follow.
It moves potassium into the cells in 15 to 30 minutes, but with ECG changes the heart is protected first.
It takes hours to work, far too slow now.
He makes little urine on dialysis, so a water tablet won't remove potassium.

lq: What is given first for high potassium with ECG changes?

q: What was the injection?
s: Mr. Raouf, 76, has Parkinson's disease that is well controlled on his tablets. He was admitted with a urine infection and became confused and agitated at night. The night doctor gave him an injection to calm him. By morning he was stiff all over, could not get out of bed and could hardly swallow. His Parkinson's tablets were all given on time.
c: Parkinson's disease, an injection for agitation, then sudden stiffness all over.

a.w: It blocks dopamine, which a Parkinson's brain is already short of. It can freeze movement and should be avoided.
It can cause drowsiness and falls, but it doesn't block dopamine or cause stiffness.
The antibiotic for his infection. It doesn't cause stiffness.
It treats fever and pain and can't make him stiff.

lq: Which calming drug should be avoided in Parkinson's disease?

q: What is in the drip?
s: Reem, 24, is 36 weeks pregnant with her first baby. She has a bad headache, flashing lights and swollen hands. Her pressure is 170/112 and her urine is full of protein. Then she has a fit. She is given a drip to stop more fits. Over the next hours a nurse checks her knee reflexes again and again and counts her breathing every hour.
c: Fits late in pregnancy with high pressure, and staff checking her reflexes and breathing.

a.w: It prevents and treats eclamptic fits. Too much stops the reflexes and breathing, so both are checked.
It stops a fit but is worse than magnesium at preventing more in eclampsia, and needs no reflex checks.
It is less effective than magnesium in eclampsia.
It starts labor or tightens the womb after birth. It doesn't stop fits.

lq: Which drug prevents and treats eclamptic fits?

q: Which eye drop is making her wheeze?
s: Mrs. Nadia, 66, was told the pressure in her eyes is high and was started on drops twice a day. A week later her old asthma flared up: she wheezes at night and uses her blue inhaler more often. She hasn't had a cold and nothing at home has changed. Her eye pressure has come down nicely.
c: High eye pressure, new drops, and asthma flaring within a week.

a.w: A beta-blocker. Enough is absorbed through the eye to tighten the airways in asthma.
It can darken the iris and lengthen the lashes, but it doesn't cause wheeze.
It can cause tiredness and red, itchy eyes, not wheeze.
It leaves a bitter taste and doesn't affect the airways.

lq: Which glaucoma drops can make asthma worse?

q: What weekly tablet was she taking?
s: Mrs. Laila, 70, has taken a weekly tablet for thin bones for nine years, standing up with a full glass of water. For a few weeks she has had an ache in her right thigh. Today she broke her thigh bone just stepping off a curb. The X-ray shows a short, straight break across the middle of the bone, with thickening on its outer side.
c: Nine years of a weekly bone tablet taken upright with water, a thigh ache, then a straight break.

a.w: Long use of bisphosphonates can cause rare unusual thigh fractures, often after a thigh ache. That is why some patients take a break after five years.
It isn't a weekly tablet and doesn't cause unusual fractures.
Also weekly, but for arthritis, and it doesn't cause this fracture.
It thins the bones, but it is taken daily and causes ordinary fractures of the spine and hip.

lq: Which long-term bone drugs can cause an unusual thigh fracture?

q: What did the doctor give him?
s: Ziad, 2, woke at night with a barking cough like a seal and a harsh noise when he breathes in. He had a runny nose for two days before. He is pink and alert, with mild pulling-in under the ribs. The doctor gave him a single dose of medicine by mouth. An hour later the harsh noise had gone at rest and he went home.
c: A barking cough and harsh breathing in after a cold, better after one dose by mouth.

a.w: One dose of steroid by mouth calms the airway swelling in croup within hours.
Croup is caused by a virus, so antibiotics don't help.
It opens the small airways in wheeze, but croup is swelling in the upper airway.
It doesn't treat the swelling and isn't advised for small children.

lq: What is given for croup?
la: A single dose of oral dexamethasone

q: Which long-term tablet became toxic?
s: Mr. Tarek, 45, has taken a mood tablet for bipolar disorder for six years, with blood levels checked often. He sprained his ankle and took ibuprofen three times a day for a week. Now he has a coarse tremor, diarrhea and an unsteady walk, and he is confused. His kidney numbers have risen a little.
c: A mood tablet with regular blood levels, a week of ibuprofen, then tremor, diarrhea and confusion.

a.w: Ibuprofen slows how the kidneys clear lithium, so its level rises to toxic: tremor, diarrhea, unsteadiness and confusion.
With ibuprofen it raises the risk of bleeding, not tremor and confusion like this.
It causes weight gain and sleepiness and isn't checked by blood levels.
Its level is sometimes checked, but ibuprofen doesn't push it up this way.

lq: Which common painkillers can push lithium to toxic levels?

q: What was he given too much of?
s: Mr. Fouad, 70, has severe COPD. The ambulance crew found him breathless with an oxygen level of 82%. They gave him oxygen through a tight mask at the highest flow. By arrival he is sleepy and hard to wake, with warm hands and a bounding pulse. His oxygen now reads 99%, but his blood gas shows high carbon dioxide and acid.
c: Severe COPD, top-flow oxygen, then 99% with drowsiness and high carbon dioxide.

a.w: In some COPD patients, high oxygen raises carbon dioxide and makes them drowsy. The target is 88 to 92%.
Too much causes a fast heart, tremor and low potassium, not sleepiness.
It could do the same, but he wasn't given any. The story shows only oxygen.
It causes a dry mouth and doesn't raise carbon dioxide.

lq: What oxygen target is used in COPD patients who hold carbon dioxide?

q: Which lupus tablet did the gout tablet make toxic?
s: Mrs. Dalia, 44, has lupus kept quiet by a tablet that spares her steroids, with a blood count every three months. She had painful gout in her big toe again, and a new doctor started a tablet to lower her uric acid. Three weeks later she has mouth ulcers and a fever, and her white cells and platelets have dropped very low.
c: A steroid-sparing lupus tablet, a new gout tablet, then the blood count crashed.

a.w: Allopurinol blocks the enzyme that breaks azathioprine down, so its level rises and wipes out the bone marrow.
It needs eye checks, not blood counts, and doesn't interact with allopurinol.
It can lower the blood count too, but allopurinol doesn't raise its level.
It doesn't interact with allopurinol and doesn't drop the white cells.

lq: Which gout drug must not be given with azathioprine at full dose?

q: What operation did he have after the crash?
s: Mr. Wael, 35, had a car crash at 20 and needed an emergency operation for bleeding in his belly. He was told then to have some vaccines but never did. Today he has a fever, and within hours his pressure falls and purple spots spread over his skin. His blood cultures grow pneumococcus. His blood film shows small dots inside the red cells.
c: Belly bleeding after a crash, missed vaccines, sudden pneumococcal sepsis and dots in the red cells.

a.w: Without a spleen, the body can't clear capsule bacteria like pneumococcus, so sepsis is fast and deadly. The dots are Howell-Jolly bodies.
It doesn't leave him open to pneumococcus or put dots in the red cells.
It can cause bowel problems, not overwhelming infection years later.
Living with one kidney doesn't weaken him against infection.

lq: Which vaccines are needed after a splenectomy?
la: Pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib, plus a yearly flu vaccine

q: What should be done first?
s: At a family lunch, Lina, 8 months old, was eating soft pieces of apple when she suddenly went silent. She can't cry or cough, and her face turns red, then blue around the lips. She is still awake, looking at her mother and waving her arms. Her uncle, who did a first aid course, rushes over to help.
t: Back blows for a choking baby
c: An awake baby who suddenly can't cry or cough: severe choking.

a.w: In a choking baby who is awake, give up to 5 back blows, then 5 chest thrusts, and repeat.
They can injure a baby's liver. They are used only over 1 year of age.
It can push the food deeper. Only remove what you can see.
Only when she stops responding.

lq: What is the first step for a choking baby who is still awake?
la: Up to 5 back blows, then 5 chest thrusts
